title: Nabal, Abigail, and the Blood David Did Not Shed
summary: Samuel dies and is mourned by all Israel. David asks a rich herdsman named Nabal for provisions at shearing time, is insulted, and sets out with four hundred men to wipe out Nabal's household. Nabal's wife Abigail intercepts him with gifts and a speech that turns him back from bloodshed; ten days later the LORD strikes Nabal dead, and David marries Abigail.
story: The chapter opens with a death that closes an era. Samuel, the last judge and the prophet who anointed both Saul and David, is buried at Ramah, and the story will go on without him. It sits between two scenes in which David has Saul at his mercy and refuses to kill him (chapters 24 and 26). Here the temptation comes from a different direction. Nabal is no king, and David's anger at him is personal, the rage of a man whose favors have been scorned. In chapter 24 David restrained himself; in this chapter he has to be restrained by someone else. The episode shows how near the future king came to staining his hands with the kind of blood that would have disqualified him, and it introduces Abigail, the first person in the book outside Jonathan to say aloud that David will rule Israel.
historical:
The events belong to the years when David was an outlaw in the southern wilderness of Judah, hiding from Saul with a band of around six hundred men, probably in the last years of Saul's reign in the late eleventh century BC. Maon and Carmel here are small towns in the hill country south of Hebron, not the Mount Carmel on the northern coast. The Wilderness of Paran lies far to the south in the Sinai; the Greek Septuagint reads Maon at verse 1, which many scholars think fits the setting better.

Nabal is called a Calebite, a member of the clan descended from Caleb, the spy who had received Hebron and its region as his inheritance (Joshua 14). The Calebites were the leading clan in exactly the area where David was living. That matters: when David later marries Nabal's widow and is crowned at Hebron (2 Samuel 2), he has ties to the landowning families of that district. The note at the end that David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel (a town in Judah, not the northern Jezreel) and that Saul had given Michal to another man shows David's household taking shape apart from Saul's.
cultural:
Sheep-shearing was a festival in the pastoral calendar, a time of feasting and generosity when the year's wool was cashed in (compare Judah in Genesis 38 and Absalom in 2 Samuel 13). David's request comes on a day of plenty, and it rests on a real service: his men had camped near Nabal's herdsmen in open country where raiders roamed, and neither stolen nor harmed them. Nabal's own shepherd says they were a wall around us day and night. In that world, protection given was expected to be repaid with a gift, and David's greeting is courteous, even calling himself your son David. Nabal's reply is a calculated insult. By asking who David is and hinting that he is a runaway slave, he denies him any standing at all.

Abigail's gift is large, the food of a feast loaded on donkeys (a seah was a dry measure, roughly a third of an ephah). Her posture is that of a petitioner before a ruler: she dismounts, falls on her face, and takes the blame on herself. The image in verse 29 of a life bound up in the bundle of the living draws on the practice of tying valuables in a pouch to keep them safe. Its opposite, enemies slung away like stones, would have made anyone who knew the story of Goliath smile.
literary: The chapter is built around speeches, and Abigail's (verses 24-31) is the longest speech by a woman in the books of Samuel. It moves from apology to theology to prophecy: she names Nabal's folly, reframes David's intended revenge as bloodshed the LORD has kept him from, and then speaks of the lasting dynasty the LORD will give him. The narrator plays constantly on names. Nabal means fool, and Abigail says so outright: “he lives up to his name: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.” Many readers also hear a pun in Calebite, which sounds like the Hebrew for dog. The chapter mirrors chapters 24 and 26: Nabal holds “a feast fit for a king”, and like Saul he repays good with evil. The difference is that God removes Nabal himself, showing David what he will later say of Saul, that the LORD strikes down in his own time.

outline.t: A servant warns Abigail, and David vows revenge
David blesses God for restraining him
David marries Abigail; his other wives

doctrines.note: God works here through an ordinary person's quick wisdom. Abigail's intervention is what the LORD uses to hold David back, and David recognizes it: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day.” Providence does not bypass human action but often works through it.

Vengeance belongs to the LORD. David is kept from avenging himself, and the LORD himself deals with Nabal. The chapter teaches the principle Paul later draws from Deuteronomy, that God's people are to leave room for his judgment rather than take it into their own hands.

Abigail and Nabal are living portraits of the wise and the foolish of Proverbs. Folly here is not low intelligence but a moral refusal to see and honor what is true, and it destroys the fool. Wisdom sees what God is doing and acts with speed and humility.

words.note: Nevalah, folly, from the same root as the name Nabal. In the Old Testament this is a strong word, used for disgraceful acts such as sexual outrage (Genesis 34:7, 2 Samuel 13:12) and for godless contempt. It is not mere silliness. Nabal's folly is his refusal to acknowledge debt, kindness, or God's purposes, and Abigail's use of the word shows she sees how serious it is.

Dam, blood. Used three times (verses 26, 31, 33) for the bloodshed Abigail keeps David from. In Israel's law, innocent blood defiled the land and brought guilt on whoever shed it. A king who came to the throne with such blood on his hands would carry that guilt into his reign, which is why Abigail says David will have no remorse when the LORD makes him ruler.

Tseror, bundle or pouch, a small bag in which valuables or money were tied up (compare Genesis 42:35). Abigail's picture of David's life bound in the bundle of the living means God keeps him as a treasure. Later Jewish tradition drew on this phrase for prayers at burial, but in context it speaks of God preserving David's life now.

Aman, to be firm or faithful, the root behind amen. In verse 28 it describes the lasting dynasty (literally a firm or faithful house) the LORD will make for David. The same phrase returns in God's covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7:16, so Abigail anticipates the promise that will define David's line.

christ: Abigail is the first to speak of a firm house for David, the promise God makes formally in 2 Samuel 7 and which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David. The chapter also shows the kind of king the Messiah must be. David's instinct is to avenge an insult with a sword; the LORD holds him back so that his throne will not rest on needless bloodshed. The link to Christ here is thematic, not predictive: Jesus, the son of David, taught his followers not to repay evil for evil and, when he was reviled, did not retaliate but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Some readers also see in Abigail, who takes the blame on herself to turn away wrath from a guilty household, a faint picture of intercession, though the text itself does not press that.

hard.q: Was David running a protection racket, and was his anger justified?
hard.a: Some modern readers see David's request as a shakedown: an armed band offers protection and threatens violence when unpaid. The text gives reasons to read it otherwise. Nabal's own servant confirms that David's men were a real defense and took nothing, and a gift at shearing time was customary. David's request is polite and leaves the amount to Nabal. At the same time, the narrator does not defend David's response. His vow to kill every male in Nabal's household is disproportionate and would have punished servants who had done nothing, which is exactly why Abigail calls it bloodshed and why David thanks God for stopping him. The chapter treats David's grievance as real and his planned revenge as sin. That honesty about the future king's temper is typical of Samuel.

questions: Abigail acts quickly, humbly, and at personal risk to stop a disaster. Where might wisdom call you to step between someone's anger and the harm it is about to do?
David was right that Nabal had wronged him and wrong about what to do about it. How do you tell the difference between a real grievance and a right to revenge?
Nabal refused to see what he owed others. What makes it hard for comfortable people to recognize the kindness they have received?
